passed.title: Series.count counts NaN as a valid value; only nulls are excluded
passed.trap: `Series.count` returns the number of non-null elements. A floating-point NaN is not null in Polars, so it is counted. pandas users expect `count()` to skip NaN, so they get a larger number than they expect. Use `Series.len` for the total length. To count only real numbers, first convert NaN to null with `Series.fill_nan(None)`, then call `Series.count`.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

s = pl.Series("a", [1.0, None, float("nan")])
print("len:", s.len())
print("count (NaN counted):", s.count())
print("count excluding NaN:", s.fill_nan(None).count())
passed.output:
len: 3
count (NaN counted): 2
count excluding NaN: 1

passed.title: drop_nulls keeps NaN and drop_nans keeps null
passed.trap: In Polars, null (missing) and NaN (a float value) are different things. `Series.drop_nulls` leaves NaN in place, and `Series.drop_nans` leaves nulls in place. pandas `dropna` removes both, so translating it to one of these methods leaves bad values behind. Chain both calls when you want to remove both kinds.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

s = pl.Series("a", [1.0, None, 3.0, float("nan")])
print("drop_nulls:", s.drop_nulls().to_list())
print("drop_nans:", s.drop_nans().to_list())
print("both:", s.drop_nulls().drop_nans().to_list())

passed.title: Use eq_missing when null should compare equal to null
passed.trap: `Series.eq` (and `==`) propagates nulls. Comparing null with null gives null, not `True`. If you use that mask as a filter, the null rows are silently dropped. Use `Series.eq_missing` when two missing values should count as a match. It always returns a non-null boolean.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

s1 = pl.Series("a", [333, 200, None])
s2 = pl.Series("a", [100, 200, None])
print("eq:", s1.eq(s2).to_list())
print("eq_missing:", s1.eq_missing(s2).to_list())
print("matches via eq:", s1.filter(s1.eq(s2)).len())
print("matches via eq_missing:", s1.filter(s1.eq_missing(s2)).len())
passed.output:
eq: [False, True, None]
eq_missing: [False, True, True]
matches via eq: 1
matches via eq_missing: 2

passed.title: Series.equals ignores names and dtypes by default
passed.trap: `Series.equals` defaults to `check_dtypes=False`, `check_names=False` and `null_equal=True`. Two Series with different names and different integer dtypes can therefore compare as equal. If you use it as a strict test, pass `check_dtypes=True` and `check_names=True`. Note that the old `strict` parameter was renamed `check_dtypes`. Pass `null_equal=False` if nulls should make the comparison fail.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

a = pl.Series("a", [1, 2, None])
b = pl.Series("b", [1, 2, None], dtype=pl.Int32)
print("default:", a.equals(b))
print("strict:", a.equals(b, check_dtypes=True, check_names=True))
print("null_equal=False:", a.equals(b, null_equal=False))
passed.output:
default: True
strict: False
null_equal=False: False

passed.title: Series.extend mutates the original Series in place
passed.trap: `Series.extend` appends the other Series' data into this Series' own memory. It modifies the Series in place and returns it only for convenience. Writing `b = a.extend(other)` therefore also changes `a`, which breaks the pandas habit that methods return new objects. Call `Series.clone` first, or use `pl.concat`, if `a` must stay unchanged.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

a = pl.Series("a", [1, 2, 3])
b = a.extend(pl.Series("b", [4, 5]))
print("a after extend:", a.to_list())
print("b is a:", b is a)

c = pl.Series("c", [1, 2, 3])
d = c.clone().extend(pl.Series("x", [4, 5]))
print("c untouched:", c.to_list(), "d:", d.to_list())
e = pl.concat([c, pl.Series("c", [9])])
print("c untouched:", c.to_list(), "e:", e.to_list())
passed.output:
a after extend: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
b is a: True
c untouched: [1, 2, 3] d: [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
c untouched: [1, 2, 3] e: [1, 2, 3, 9]

passed.title: Series.cut bins are right-closed by default and labels need len(breaks)+1 entries
passed.trap: `Series.cut` (unstable) uses right-closed intervals by default, so a value exactly equal to a break falls into the lower bin. Pass `left_closed=True` to make bins left-closed. `labels` must have exactly one more entry than `breaks`; a mismatch raises an error. The result is `Categorical`, or a `Struct` if `include_breaks=True`, not a string column.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

s = pl.Series("x", [-1, 0, 1, 2])
print(s.cut([0, 1]).cast(pl.String).to_list())
print(s.cut([0, 1], left_closed=True).cast(pl.String).to_list())
print(s.cut([0, 1]).dtype)
try:
    s.cut([0, 1], labels=["lo", "hi"])
except Exception as e:
    print(type(e))
print(s.cut([0, 1], labels=["lo", "mid", "hi"]).cast(pl.String).to_list())

passed.title: Series.cum_count counts non-null values; it is not a row number
passed.trap: `Series.cum_count` returns the running count of non-null values, starting at 1. When it hits a null, the count stays flat. Do not use it as a 0-based row index that counts every row. For row positions, use `DataFrame.with_row_index`.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

s = pl.Series("s", ["x", "k", None, "d"])
print("cum_count:", s.cum_count().to_list())
row = s.to_frame().with_row_index("row").get_column("row")
print("row index:", row.to_list())

passed.title: Series.describe uses nearest-rank percentiles by default, not linear interpolation
passed.trap: `Series.describe` defaults to `interpolation='nearest'`, so its 25%/50%/75% rows are picked from actual data points. If you expect linearly interpolated percentiles, the numbers can differ. Pass `interpolation="linear"` to get interpolated percentiles. The output is a two-column DataFrame (`statistic`, `value`), not an indexed Series.
passed.example:
import polars as pl

s = pl.Series("a", [1, 2, 3, 4])
pct = pl.col("statistic").str.ends_with("%")
print(s.describe().columns)
print("nearest:", s.describe().filter(pct).rows())
print("linear:", s.describe(interpolation="linear").filter(pct).rows())
